title: House Robber II
problemStatement:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. All houses at this place are arranged in a circle. That means the first house is the neighbor of the last one. Meanwhile, adjacent houses have a security system connected and it will automatically contact the police if two adjacent houses were broken into on the same night.

Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money of each house, return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

examples.explanation: You cannot rob house 1 (money = 2) and then rob house 3 (money = 2), because they are adjacent houses. Rob house 2 (money = 3) for maximum amount.
Rob house 1 (money = 1) and then rob house 3 (money = 3). Total amount you can rob = 1 + 3 = 4.
You cannot rob house 1 and house 3 because house 1 and house 3 are adjacent (circular). Rob house 3 (money = 3).

solutions.detailedExplanation: This recursive solution handles the circular constraint by tracking whether the first house (index 0) was robbed using a boolean flag. The key insight is that if we rob the first house, we cannot rob the last house. The flag propagates this constraint through the recursion. At each house, we have two choices: skip it (recurse to i+1), or rob it (add nums[i] and recurse to i+2, setting the flag if i==0). The base case returns 0 when we go beyond the array bounds or when the flag is true and we reach the last house (can't rob it). We try two scenarios: starting from house 0 with flag=true, and starting from house 1 with flag=false, then return the maximum. This explores all valid combinations but has exponential time complexity due to overlapping subproblems.
commonMistakes: Not handling the single house case separately (array access errors)
Forgetting to set the flag when robbing house 0 (incorrect constraint enforcement)
Not preventing robbing last house when flag is true (violates circular constraint)
Only trying one starting position instead of both (missing optimal solution)
Confusing the flag logic (should be set on i==0, not i==1)
solutions.whyItWorks: The solution correctly models the circular constraint by using a flag to track first house robbery. When we rob house 0, the flag ensures we cannot rob the last house (which is adjacent in circular arrangement). By trying both starting positions (house 0 with constraint, and house 1 without constraint from house 0), we explore all valid scenarios. The recursion correctly explores all combinations of robbing/skipping houses while respecting the no-adjacent-houses rule and the circular constraint.
keyInsights: Circular constraint: if rob first house, cannot rob last house
Flag tracks whether first house was robbed to enforce constraint
Must try both scenarios: start from house 0 (with constraint) or house 1 (without)
Base case prevents robbing last house when flag is set
Exponential time due to overlapping subproblems being recomputed

example1.explanation: Try dfs(0, true): can rob 0 (value 2) or skip. If rob 0, dfs(2, true) returns 0 (flag prevents robbing last house). If skip, dfs(1, true) robs house 1 (value 3). So dfs(0, true) = max(3, 2+0) = 3. Try dfs(1, false): rob house 1 (value 3), dfs(3, false) returns 0. Or skip house 1, dfs(2, false) robs house 2 (value 2). So dfs(1, false) = max(2, 3+0) = 3. Return max(3, 3) = 3.

example2.explanation: Try dfs(0, true): explores paths with house 0 robbed. Optimal: rob houses 0 and 2 (1+3=4, cannot rob house 3 due to flag). Try dfs(1, false): explores paths without house 0 constraint. Can rob houses 1 and 3 (2+1=3). Return max(4, 3) = 4.

solutions.detailedExplanation: This memoized solution adds a 2D cache to the recursive approach. The memo array has dimensions [n][2] where memo[i][flag] stores the maximum money that can be robbed starting from house i with the given flag value. Before computing a result, we check if it's already cached. If so, we return it immediately. Otherwise, we compute it recursively and store it in the cache. The flag dimension captures whether we're in a scenario where the first house was robbed (flag=1) or not (flag=0). This transforms the exponential recursive tree into a linear computation because each of the 2n unique states is computed exactly once. The space complexity is O(n) for the memo array plus O(n) for recursion stack depth.
commonMistakes: Using 1D memo array instead of 2D (doesn't capture the flag dimension)
Not initializing memo properly (undefined behavior)
Forgetting to store result in memo before returning (no benefit from memoization)
Incorrect memo indexing for boolean flag (need to convert true/false to 0/1)
Not checking memo before making recursive calls (defeating the purpose)
solutions.whyItWorks: Memoization eliminates redundant computation by caching results for each unique (position, flag) state. Since there are only n positions and 2 flag values, we have at most 2n unique states. Each state is computed once and then cached. Subsequent encounters of the same state return the cached value in O(1) time. This reduces the time complexity from O(2^n) to O(n) while maintaining the same correctness as the pure recursive solution.
keyInsights: 2D memoization: position and flag together determine unique state
At most 2n unique states to compute (n positions × 2 flag values)
Each state computed exactly once, then cached for reuse
Same correctness as recursion but exponential to linear time improvement
Flag dimension essential to correctly handle circular constraint

solutions.detailedExplanation: This elegant solution recognizes that the circular constraint creates exactly two scenarios: either we rob the first house (and therefore cannot rob the last), or we don't rob the first house (and can consider the last). We split the problem into two linear House Robber subproblems: (1) houses 1 to n-1 (excluding first house), and (2) houses 0 to n-2 (excluding last house). The helper function solves the standard linear House Robber problem using dynamic programming: dp[i] represents the maximum money that can be robbed from houses 0 to i. The recurrence is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2]) - either skip the current house or rob it (and skip the previous). We solve both subproblems and return the maximum. This approach is cleaner than tracking flags and naturally handles the circular constraint.

Forgetting to consider both scenarios (only checking one slice)
Incorrect array slicing (off-by-one errors in slice indices)
Not handling empty array in helper (though won't occur from main function)
Incorrect DP recurrence in helper function
Forgetting that dp[1] should be max(nums[0], nums[1]), not just nums[1]
solutions.whyItWorks: The solution correctly handles the circular constraint by recognizing mutual exclusivity: we cannot rob both the first and last houses. By considering both scenarios (rob houses 1 to n-1, or rob houses 0 to n-2) and taking the maximum, we're guaranteed to find the optimal solution while avoiding the first-last adjacency. The helper function correctly solves the linear subproblem using the standard House Robber DP approach. Since we solve two O(n) subproblems, the total time complexity is O(n).
keyInsights: Circular constraint reduces to two linear subproblems
Cannot rob both first and last house - consider both scenarios
Reuse standard House Robber DP solution for each scenario
Cleaner than flag-based approaches - no special case handling during DP
Two O(n) subproblems give O(n) total time complexity

solutions.detailedExplanation: This space-optimized solution uses the same two-scenario approach as the bottom-up solution but optimizes the helper function to use O(1) space. The key observation is that when computing dp[i], we only need the two previous values: dp[i-1] and dp[i-2]. We maintain two variables: rob1 (equivalent to dp[i-2]) and rob2 (equivalent to dp[i-1]). For each house, we compute the maximum of robbing it (rob1 + num) or skipping it (rob2), store this in newRob, then slide our window forward by updating rob1 = rob2 and rob2 = newRob. After processing all houses, rob2 contains the maximum money for that subproblem. The main function still considers nums[0] separately as a third scenario to handle edge cases, then returns the maximum of all three scenarios. This achieves O(1) space complexity (excluding input slices) while maintaining O(n) time complexity.
commonMistakes: Not updating variables in correct order (need temp variable or careful sequencing)
Forgetting to consider nums[0] as a separate scenario in main function
Incorrect initialization of rob1 and rob2 (should both be 0)
Updating rob1 before computing newRob (race condition)
Not understanding the sliding window pattern (rob1 and rob2 represent dp[i-2] and dp[i-1])
solutions.whyItWorks: The space optimization works because the DP recurrence only looks back two positions. By maintaining a sliding window of the last two DP values, we can compute each new value without storing the entire array. The variables rob1 and rob2 effectively track dp[i-2] and dp[i-1], and we compute dp[i] = max(rob1 + nums[i], rob2). Sliding the window forward (rob1 = rob2, rob2 = newRob) prepares for the next iteration. This maintains the same correctness as the full DP array approach but uses constant extra space.
keyInsights: Sliding window optimization: only last two DP values needed
rob1 tracks dp[i-2], rob2 tracks dp[i-1], compute dp[i] on the fly
Same two-scenario approach as bottom-up but with O(1) space per scenario
Separate check for nums[0] handles edge case where single house is optimal
Optimal space-time trade-off: O(n) time, O(1) space
